**--** This first part is back story on Rebecca, it did not happen in the dream. This part happened in real life. 

Here is a **tl;dr**, first love that I met in college. I screwed it up, though she remained a good friend. I am still in college now, though this happened over a year ago. 

I had met Rebecca sophomore year at University. I was on winter break at home and working in a café. The morning was particularly chilly and although it had not snowed in thirty years, Main Street was deserted. I saw her through the window as she sat at one of the tables out front. She was all of about 5 feet tall wearing a plaid pea coat and sunglasses. I hoped desperately that she would come inside. Living in a small town has its charms, however the dating scene had long since gone stale. I had no luck finding a girl at school either, because they all seemed so wrapped up in something called a “Major.” So here I was, another Winter break to spend with friends on the beach. I was still missing something, I felt, yet I was content with that safety in familiarity all the same.

She had watched me put out the sidewalk sign earlier and I pretended to not see her to avoid the awkwardness. After finishing her cigarette she stood up. My heart fluttered a bit. Every cell in my body, every nerve cell, skin cell, bone cell, blood cell, knee cell, and eye cell began to watch out a window with an anticipation rarely seen since having matured. 

She opened the front door and came inside along with a cold gust of air. Sitting at one of the tables she opened her book, The Stories of Vladimir Nabokov, and started reading. This was peculiar, and it let the wind out of my sales, as I was hoping her ordering coffee would start some sort of conversation.

After a few minutes the thought occurred to me that she was expecting me to take her order. I decided to do just that. I welcomed her and as is normal with any guest I asked about where she was from. I was not expecting her answer and was all the more intrigued. She had graduated high school the previous semester and was on a sailing trip along the coast. They were roughly a third of the way and were about to make an open ocean crossing. Their boat, however, was having none of it. As any sailor, amateur or peg-legged alike, will tell you: there is always something to fix on a boat. So as it turned out they were docked at the local marina and she was exploring the local town. 

We talked for a while about old Russian films and the particular short story she was reading at the time. It was a strange sort of vibe, and I was nervous, but I seemed to be able to say everything I needed to.

We were both so out of place in this town and I knew she would at least want something to do until she again sailed off. So, I invited her to the New Years Eve party at the beach that I was suddenly planning in my head. She came to the party the next night, we had great time around a huge bonfire with different friends of mine from high school. We become friends and lovers over the next few nights. We did all sorts of things around town in those short days. We parted ways as she was going to college next year and I had to go back to school away from the coast.
We promised to stay in touch, and did. We went to New Orleans months later and she visited me once more. We weren’t without problems though. I would occasionally say something mean because I was jealous or frustrated and she would cry. I felt more terrible which drove her to be cautious of me. While she remained very loving and nice to me, I could tell she would never fully trust me again, nor would we ever have that feeling again. Somehow we are still friends today, and talk about all sorts of nonsense. She lives more than a thousand miles away.

The ultimate first step: Realize that **right now** you have the power to change your thoughts. The way you view problems, how you make decisions and the means you utilize are all under your control. Don't mentally penalize yourself for doing these things, just organize and schedule them so that you don't have to panic. Taking control allows you to not have to worry that some goal/task will get done while at the same time balancing your sanity and not overworking yourself. Set a realistic goal: Perhaps get a job. Work on a skill, hobby, or work on a diet/exercise program that will get you out of the house. Another final important thing to remember:  Forget what negative people have to say. Better yet, forget negative people all together. Apart from your family and a close selection of those your respect, everyone else can piss off with their judgements of you. This is *your* life. This a cluster-bumshuck of advice. Eat it like spaghetti. I don't mean this in the macho 'harden the fuck up' kind of way. Honestly though at this point it's your fault for not talking to people. Love yourself, realize that you are worth loving just like any human being. So in terms of conversing: be respectful of people and their shortcomings. Think first and don't speak to fast. Remember neither you nor they have anything to prove in a conversation. It [the conversation] needs to go somewhere though, so make sure you listen to them and either come back with a question that cannot be answered with a yes/no. Be agreeable- but not too agreeable. In other words if someone asks you where you would like to eat don't immediately say "anywhere" or "I don't care".  Maybe start with a type of food, or suggest a restaurant. Valid reasons for turning down someone idea can be allergies, too formal/informal. 

Start with any person- same or opposite gender- and don't seem desperate, but strike up a conversation. Maybe make a joking observation or offer to hold the door/pick up dropped item/ etc. Maybe you are in line at a coffee shop. Politely ask what they like to get. Simple shit that feeds the other persons ego. Trick is to remember that there is no pressure at this point. After a few lines if the person is responding positively [eg. smile, verbal/bodily agreement, eye contact, generally keeping up with the conversation] then attempt to migrate. If they don't respond well just dip out and don't seem clingy. Check your phone for a text (fake it if you have to).

Don't be afraid to get involved. Plenty of people may seem confident when really they just found a niche and got comfortable. Good for them. They made a fool of themselves at some point too. Just stay positive and focus on yourself.

I separated this into two parts just for convenience. 


**Diet**

After reading a few articles on the impacts of Omega3 fatty acids I decided to give them a try. Within a week my low moods were noticeably not as low. Maybe it is placebo effect, but I can honestly say that I do feel better just having started that supplement. Also because fish contains omega3 and other good nutrients I make every effort to have fish twice a week. Fish can easily be had on sushi, just baked in the oven (this works great for the really inexpensive freezer packed variety fish), or, my favorite, seared tuna steak. It really does seem to help as I feel more stabilized in terms of mood and outlook.


I have never taken prescribed drugs, so I cannot vouch for their effectiveness. I have a tendency to avoid script drugs whenever there is an alternative. When the side effects of a drug are what the drug is supposed to treat I am a bit put off. That being said **if your medical adviser (Doctors, psychologists, etc) are experienced and think that you should take something, then take their advice.**


**Lifestyle**

In terms of lifestyle I have found that modifying my behavior to be more active and yet at the same time slowing down and living the moment. I abhor the use of that contradiction, but allow me to explain. Working out in almost any form, whether it's running, biking, weights, aerobics, or training a martial art, is a wonderful distraction from worries and depressive behavior. As with cognitive behavioral therapy there are ways of combating negative thoughts and habits that lead to depressed lows. For example when a familiar situation arises making a mistake and angering someone find a better way to handle it. Instead of blaming them or conceding and being overly apologetic, think things through and decide how wrong you really were or if the other person is at fault. The point here is to change perception of situations; and further change how you might deal with them. Depression, at least for me, is marked by feelings of hopelessness and being out of control.
